newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Politics, envy said behind Kalimantan violence.
newsitem.headline: Politics, envy said behind Kalimantan violence.

text.p: A dangerous mix of envy and political tensions set off widespread rioting in this city on the final day of Indonesia's election campaign, residents said on Sunday.

At least 65 and perhaps up to 79 people were killed in the violence in the capital of South Kalimantan province on Friday as security forces were slow to clamp down on early skirmishes between rival political groups, they said.

Some fires still burned and smoke hung in the air on Sunday in the centre of the riverside city of 400,000, described as the Venice of Indonesia for its canals, after a huge mob rampaged through its commercial heart on Friday afternoon.
Kalimantan is the Indonesian half of Borneo island.
More than 100 people were injured and a string of buildings, including hotels, churches, shopping centres and houses were gutted.

"We had no suspicions that something like this would happen. Just two days before the government had said this was one of the safest areas," the director of the Ulin general hospital, Sudarto, told Reuters.
Witnesses said they watched police remove more than 50 charred bodies from the ruins of the four-level Mitra shopping complex on Saturday.
In Jakarta, the military said the bodies of 65 people were found in the complex. Banjarmasin's Dinamika Berita newspaper said 79 people were killed, 75 of them in the Mitra complex.

Residents said the incident began with clashes involving supporters of the ruling Golkar party who paraded through the city on Friday morning, attacking people who refused to show the two-fingered V-for-Victory party sign.
Those who gave the one-fingered sign of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) in return were special targets.

Later, after Friday Islamic prayers, thousands of people poured out of the town's mosques to intercept those heading to an afternoon Golkar rally. Witnesses said some of the masses wore the PPP's green colours.

Taiyibno, 23, told Reuters from his hospital bed that he was attacked with sticks and machetes when a Golkar flag from earlier campaigning was found under his motorcycle seat when he was stopped and searched by the crowd on his way home from work.
Junaidi, father of 13-year-old Tedy, said his son had his wrist broken when hit with a stick for wearing a Golkar T-shirt that had been handed out earlier.
Witnesses said what started as political clashes rapidly deteriorated into widespread looting and rioting in the absence of authority.

"The police and military were nowhere to be seen in the early afternoon. If the problem was anticipated and they had come onto the street by 3 or 4 p.m. it could have been controlled," one witness said. "Instead, everyone looked after themselves."
Witnesses said the city's top Hotel Kalimantan was burnt after the town's most expensive shopping centre below was ransacked and then set ablaze.
"It is important to note that they were looting," Kalimantan military commander Major-General Namori Anoen told reporters on Saturday, adding police had detained 181 people.
Witnesses said many of those leading the rioting were carrying sickles, which are popular among migrants from nearby Madura island, who are mostly labourers or tricycle taxi operators.

They pointed to the gap between the rich and poor as fuel for the rioting and said the small minority of Chinese, who dominate commercial life, and the generally well-educated and better off Christians were easy targets for further violence.
Similar envy and frustration has been cited as the reason for a string of ethnic riots on the country's main Java island in the past 12 months.

One member of the burnt out Batak Protestant church in the centre of Banjarmasin shrugged when asked what had fuelled the attack. "It's all the same as on Java. I don't need to explain it. We used to have no problems," he said.
A Chinese woman, sifting through the ashes of her house, said rioters were envious of the economic wealth of her community.
"The burning of the church was just a side-effect. The Chinese houses were next to it," said another resident.
